The Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI) is the official count of work-related deaths
from injuries in the United States, produced by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). In this
notebook you will explore who dies at work, how, and in which jobs. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The tables in `data/tidy/` are complete (not samples) and are committed to the repository.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/us-bls-cfoi/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name), show_col_types = FALSE)
}

national <- read_tidy("cfoi_national.csv")   # counts by characteristic, 2011-2022
by_detail <- read_tidy("cfoi_by_detail.csv") # counts by industry, occupation, event, source
states <- read_tidy("cfoi_states.csv")       # counts by state
rates <- read_tidy("cfoi_rates.csv")         # rates per 100,000 FTE workers, 2023-2024
```

# Part 1. How many workers die each year?

```{r totals}
totals <- national |> filter(group == "All")
totals

rates |> filter(section == "Total")

ggplot(totals, aes(year, fatalities)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Fatal occupational injuries in the US", x = NULL, y = "Deaths")
```

**Questions**

1. About how many workers died from work injuries each year? What happened in 2020, and why?
2. CFOI counts deaths from **injuries**, not illnesses. Name two types of work-related deaths
   that CFOI does not count. Why are they harder to count?
3. CFOI confirms each death with at least two independent sources (for example death
   certificates, workers' compensation reports, OSHA reports, news). Why does that make it more
   complete than a system based on employer reports?

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. How do workers die?

```{r events}
events <- by_detail |> filter(detail_type == "event", display_level == 1)

ggplot(events, aes(year, fatalities, colour = label)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Fatal work injuries by event or exposure", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")

events |>
  filter(year == max(year)) |>
  mutate(share = round(100 * fatalities / sum(fatalities), 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(fatalities)) |>
  select(label, fatalities, share)
```

**Questions**

1. What is the leading cause of death at work? Is that what you expected?
2. Which event categories are increasing? Pick one and suggest an explanation.

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Who dies at work?

```{r who}
latest <- max(national$year)

national |>
  filter(group %in% c("Gender", "Age group", "Worker status"), year == latest) |>
  select(group, category, fatalities)

national |>
  filter(group == "Race", year == latest) |>
  arrange(desc(fatalities)) |>
  select(category, fatalities) |>
  head(8)
```

Counts depend on how many people work in each group. **Rates** take that into account:

```{r who-rates}
rates |>
  filter(section %in% c("Employee status", "Sex", "Age", "Race or ethnic origin")) |>
  select(year, section, characteristic, rate_per_100k_fte) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = rate_per_100k_fte, names_prefix = "rate_")
```

**Questions**

1. How many times higher is the fatal injury rate for men than for women? For self-employed
   compared with wage and salary workers? Why might self-employed workers be at higher risk?
2. How do rates change with age? Why are older workers at higher risk of dying from an injury?
3. Hispanic or Latino workers have a higher rate than other groups. What factors could explain
   this (think about industries, occupations, language, and immigration status)?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Most deaths vs. most dangerous

```{r occupations}
# Occupations with the most deaths (count), latest year
by_detail |>
  filter(detail_type == "occupation", display_level == 4, year == latest) |>
  arrange(desc(fatalities)) |>
  select(label, fatalities) |>
  head(10)

# Occupations with the highest rates, latest year with rates
rates |>
  filter(section == "Occupation", year == max(year)) |>
  arrange(desc(rate_per_100k_fte)) |>
  select(characteristic, hours_millions, rate_per_100k_fte, margin_of_error) |>
  head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. Which occupation has the most deaths? Which has the highest rate? Why are they different?
2. If you were a policymaker with a limited budget, would you focus on the occupations with the
   most deaths or the highest rates? Make a case for each.

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. States

```{r states, fig.height = 8}
states |>
  filter(group == "All", area_type == "State or DC", year == latest) |>
  ggplot(aes(fatalities, fct_reorder(state, fatalities))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = paste("Fatal work injuries by state,", latest), x = "Deaths", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which states have the most deaths? Why is this not a fair comparison of how safe work is?
2. New York appears three times in `states` (New York City, the rest of the state, and both
   combined). Why is it important to check this before adding up states?
